claims.text: Rapid quenching AlCoCrFeNi from above 1100°C produces a fully disordered, high-entropy state.
Annealing AlCoCrFeNi at 700°C for approximately 24 hours promotes partial atomic ordering.
High mixing entropy in fully disordered AlCoCrFeNi resists phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
High mixing entropy in fully disordered AlCoCrFeNi resists intermetallic formation during high-temperature exposure.
Partial ordering induced by extended annealing promotes intermetallic-phase formation.
Annealing-induced intermetallic phases accelerate degradation at high temperature.
Processing under ultra-high-purity inert atmospheres eliminates oxidation effects.
High mixing entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
A fully disordered state suppresses diffusion pathways.
Suppression of phase separation and diffusion pathways improves resistance to grain coarsening.
Suppression of phase separation and diffusion pathways improves oxidation resistance.
Intermetallic phases in the partially ordered state create additional diffusion routes.
Additional diffusion routes accelerate structural degradation and chemical reactivity at high temperature.
After exposure at 700–800°C, the quenched sample will retain a more uniform, single-phase structure than the annealed sample.
After exposure at 700–800°C, the quenched sample will exhibit less grain coarsening than the annealed sample.
After exposure at 700–800°C, the quenched sample will exhibit less oxidation than the annealed sample.
The annealed sample will contain more XRD- or TEM-detectable intermetallic phases than the quenched sample.
The stabilizing effect attributed to high mixing entropy is significant below approximately 800°C.
At temperatures significantly above 800°C, both initial states may degrade regardless of their initial ordering.

contradictions.description: The intervention says the ultra-high-purity inert atmosphere will eliminate oxidation effects, but oxidation and oxidation-derived weight gain are subsequently treated as comparative outcomes and falsification criteria. If oxidation is eliminated, it cannot distinguish the two states.
